analysis.one_liner: Restores labels telling shoppers which country their beef comes from.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2025 with 11 bipartisan Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and has not received a committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: Beef sold in US grocery stores can come from cattle raised in other countries, and shoppers often cannot tell. This bill would bring back mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef — including ground beef — so retailers must say where the meat was produced. Because an earlier version of this labeling rule was struck down in a World Trade Organization dispute, the bill directs the US trade office and the Agriculture Department to design a version that complies with WTO rules and put it in place within a year.
analysis.who_benefits: American cattle ranchers gain a clearer competitive footing against imported beef, since shoppers who prefer US-raised beef can actually identify it. Grocery shoppers gain the right to know where their beef was born, raised, and slaughtered — information the current labeling rules largely do not provide for beef.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US cattle ranchers and grocery shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Agricultural Marketing Act to add beef, including ground beef, to the mandatory country-of-origin labeling requirements that already cover other meats, so retailers must tell customers where beef comes from.

Because a previous mandatory labeling rule ran into a WTO dispute, the bill requires the US Trade Representative and USDA to design and implement a WTO-compliant way of reinstating beef labeling within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers and retailers would bear the cost of tracking and labeling beef by origin, and imported beef would become less attractive to label-conscious shoppers. Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers through slightly higher beef prices.

drawbacks.text: Tracking cattle through the supply chain to label origin costs money for packers and retailers, and some of that cost is likely to show up in beef prices at the store.

A prior US mandatory country-of-origin rule for beef was challenged by Canada and Mexico at the World Trade Organization and ultimately repealed by Congress after the WTO authorized retaliatory tariffs; the bill asks the trade office to find a WTO-compliant approach, which may prove difficult and could narrow how informative the labels can be.
The bill relies on the US Trade Representative and USDA to work out the details within fixed deadlines, so the actual labels shoppers see depend on how those agencies implement the mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — shoppers knowing where their beef comes from and US ranchers competing on equal footing against unlabeled imports — is real but modest in dollar terms. The main costs are supply-chain labeling compliance and the risk of new trade friction if a WTO-compliant design proves hard to craft. On balance it is a transparency measure whose costs fall mostly on a concentrated meatpacking sector, not on shoppers directly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote ever since.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the American Beef Labeling Act on February 5, 2025, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats Cory Booker, Martin Heinrich, and John Fetterman and Republicans Mike Rounds, Cynthia Lummis, and John Hoeven.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day it was introduced.
Eleven senators in total are listed as cosponsors — 4 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and 7 of its 55 Republicans — giving the bill bipartisan support.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral: no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers, beef importers, and retailers come out ahead so far: without a vote or a law, beef from other countries can continue reaching store shelves without origin labels, and the packers and retailers avoid the cost of tracking and labeling beef by country.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and recruited bipartisan original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee (Chair John Boozman)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in February 2025 and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill.

against.name: Major meatpacking and cattle industry groups
against.role: Industry interests that historically opposed mandatory beef origin labeling
against.what_they_did: Have long lobbied against reinstating mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef, which would raise their tracking and compliance costs and make imported beef less competitive.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines from the start — Thune introduced it alongside three Democrats and three Republicans, and the 11 cosponsors split 7 Republicans to 4 Democrats — and there is no record of organized floor opposition.

industries.note: Packers would have to track and segregate beef by country of origin to feed the labeling requirement, and imports they currently blend into the US supply would become less attractive to retailers. Their cost is the shopper's information gain, which is why their interest runs against the public's in this bill.
Origin labels let ranchers compete directly against unlabeled imported beef, since shoppers who prefer US-raised beef can finally identify it. Ranchers and consumers win together under this bill.

Retailers bear new labeling compliance costs at the meat counter, but they already must label other covered meats under the same statute, and transparent origin labels can help them sell to shoppers who want US beef.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been in the Senate Agriculture Committee since February 2025 with no hearing or markup. Similar beef-labeling bills in recent Congresses died in committee, and reinstating a rule that triggered a WTO dispute makes floor time unlikely; the realistic path is that it stays stalled unless attached to a broader agriculture or farm bill.
